passage: In the corridors of their Mumbai school, everyone knew the map: the football boys by the water cooler, the debate kids near the library, the backbenchers on the stairs. Chinmay, fifteen, belonged to the football boys. When he was paired with Ganga from the debate kids for the history project, his friends groaned. "Library people? Good luck, bro." At lunch he had to pick: his usual spot by the cooler, or the library table where Ganga was waiting with a plan. He stood in the corridor longer than he meant to. Then he went to the library. When his friends passed and whistled, his ears went red. But Ganga's plan was actually good, and by the end of the period he'd forgotten the whistling.

qa.q: Where did the football boys hang out?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay stand in the corridor longer than he meant to?
qa.a: He was torn between staying with his group and going to work with Ganga, knowing that crossing over might bring teasing.

qa.q: How could Chinmay handle his friends' whistling next time?
qa.a: Shrug it off with a light reply or explain it's a project, so the line feels less rigid without a fight.

qa.q: How might Ganga have experienced waiting at the library table?
qa.a: She might have wondered whether he would show up at all, given which group he belongs to.

grounding: It shows a teenager navigating the strict lines between school groups when a project crosses them.

passage:
"You're not sitting with us anymore?" Saurabh asked.
Francis shifted his tray. "The band guys asked me. We're planning the fest."
"So you're a band guy now."
"I play guitar, Saurabh. I've always played guitar."
"You never sat with them before."
"They never asked before." Francis sighed. "Why does it have to be one table or the other?"
"Because that's how it works here. You pick."
"Then I pick both. Monday and Wednesday with you. Tuesday and Thursday with them."
Saurabh snorted. "They'll never let you do that."
"Watch me."
But on Tuesday, when Francis sat with the band, one of them said, "Your cricket friends coming too?" and nobody laughed.

qa.q: Which days did Francis offer to sit with Saurabh?
qa.a: Monday and Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he said "So you're a band guy now"?
qa.a: Hurt and a little jealous, worried that Francis was leaving his group behind.

qa.q: What could Francis do if the band members keep making remarks?
qa.a: Answer calmly that he is friends with both, and perhaps invite Saurabh to a practice to bridge the groups.

qa.q: What does the band member's remark on Tuesday suggest about how they see groups?
qa.a: They also see people as belonging to one group, which is why the idea of two tables meets suspicion.

grounding: It shows a teenager trying to cross strict group boundaries and meeting resistance from both sides.

passage: In Class 10, our group had rules nobody said out loud. You wore the same kind of hair clips. You didn't sit with the hostel kids. You laughed at the same people. When Wasim, who'd been with us since Class 6, started sitting with the hostel boys for chess, the group froze him out. No invites, no replies in the chat. I went along with it for about a week. Then one day I saw him eating alone on the steps, and I felt sick. I sat down next to him. "Gurleen?" he said, surprised. The next morning my group had moved seats. It hurt. But looking back, that was the day I understood how tight those lines were, and that I didn't want to live inside them.

qa.q: Why did Wasim start sitting with the hostel boys?
qa.a: To play chess.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel when she saw Wasim eating alone?
qa.a: Sick and guilty about having gone along with freezing him out.

qa.q: What could Gurleen have done to make the move feel less lonely?
qa.a: Find one or two others who felt the same, or talk to a trusted adult, so as not to face the group alone.

qa.q: How might Wasim have seen Gurleen sitting down next to him?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved, since Gurleen was the first from the group to cross the line back to him.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising and stepping outside a clique's rigid rules about who belongs.

passage: Coach's note, inter-house practice, week three. Class 9 has split into two lunch groups, and it shows on the field: the 'front-row' group passes only to each other. Today Noor, who sits with that group, was put on a team with Manoj and two others from the other side. For ten minutes she hung back. Then Manoj saw her open and passed; she scored and he whooped. Afterwards I saw her glance toward her usual friends before walking off with her new teammates for water. One of her friends said something to her and she shrugged, face tight. Next step: I will mix teams by drawing lots every week, so no one has to cross over alone, and I'll keep an eye on how Noor is doing at lunch.

qa.q: How will teams be picked from next week?
qa.a: By drawing lots every week.

qa.q: What does Noor's glance toward her usual friends suggest she was worried about?
qa.a: She may have worried her friends would see walking off with the new teammates as leaving their group.

qa.q: Why might drawing lots help?
qa.a: It takes the choice out of students' hands, so mixing is not seen as betraying anyone's group.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen Noor after the goal?
qa.a: His whoop suggests he was glad to include her and saw her as a real teammate.

grounding: Shows how rigid group lines at school affect a teenager who crosses them, noticed by a coach.

passage: Friday. So Pema has been at school three weeks and still eats alone. He's actually funny; I found out in the chemistry lab when he gave all our test tubes names. Today I asked the guys if he could sit with us, and it went weird. Nobody said no. They just said 'he's not really our type' and changed the topic. What is our type? We're five boys who play the same game and wear the same shoes. I didn't push it. I hate that I didn't. Maybe on Monday I'll just go sit at his table instead. They can't kick me out of a table I leave. Or they can make it awkward forever. I'll decide on Monday. – Dhruv

qa.q: How long has Pema been at the school?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What does 'I hate that I didn't' show about Dhruv's feelings?
qa.a: He felt ashamed that he let the group's quiet refusal stand, even though he likes Pema.

qa.q: What small step could Dhruv try on Monday?
qa.a: He could sit with Pema for one lunch, or bring one friend along, to show that group lines can be crossed.

qa.q: What is lunchtime likely like for Pema right now?
qa.a: Probably lonely, eating alone while the groups around him have already formed.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager running into his group's unspoken rule about who belongs and weighing whether to cross it.
